enrichment.short_title: Milstead v Wessex Roofline: ladder footing and Construction Regulations liability
key_facts: Mr Milstead, an experienced UPVC fitter, fell from an unsecured ladder over three metres long at a domestic job in Woking on 14 May 2001 and suffered severe knee injuries.
He alleged his trainee Mr Calder failed to foot the ladder after being instructed to do so when Milstead untied it from scaffolding at the end of the day.
The defendants admitted breach of Schedule 5(2)(c) but relied on Boyle v Kodak to argue the breach was caused solely by Milstead's own acts.
The claim was commenced shortly before limitation expired, over two years after the accident.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Split trial on liability only following amendment to plead breach of statutory duty.
enrichment.outcome: Defendants held liable in negligence and for breach of statutory duty; no contributory negligence; quantum to be assessed separately if not agreed.
enrichment.ratio: Where a ladder over three metres is used unsecured, an employer is vicariously liable for a trainee's failure to foot it unless it proves the injured employee alone caused the breach; inadequate ladder training and Calder's misunderstanding of the Regulations defeated the Boyle v Kodak defence.
legal_issues: Whether Milstead instructed Calder to foot the untied ladder
Whether breach of Schedule 5(2)(c) was caused solely by Milstead
Application of Boyle v Kodak to employer training and vicarious liability
Whether Milstead was contributorily negligent

James v Hepworth & Grandage Ltd [1968] 1 QB 94

enrichment.short_title: Brookes v SYPTE: date of employer liability for hand-arm vibration syndrome
key_facts: Mr Brookes developed vibration white finger after years using pneumatic tools as a bus-fleet fitter for South Yorkshire PTE and its successor from 1982.
The recorder found the employers liable from 1975 on constructive knowledge of DD43, but the daily vibration dose exceeding 2.8 m/s² was accepted on appeal.
The employers argued they could not reasonably have known of the risk before HSE guidance in 1994.
Symptoms first appeared in 1999 and damages of £4,780 were not challenged on quantum.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Sheffield County Court on liability date and whether damages should be apportioned.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal partly allowed; liability substituted from 1989 rather than throughout employment, but full damages upheld with no apportionment because symptoms arose only after negligent exposure.
enrichment.ratio: A large transport employer with dedicated safety staff ought to have known of BS 6842 (1987) shortly after publication and to have investigated and remedied vibration exposure within about two years; the date of negligence is fact-specific and not fixed at 1989 for all transport employers.
legal_issues: When the employers ought constructively to have known of VWF risk from DD43 and BS 6842
Whether the recorder's 1975 finding was supported by evidence
Whether damages should be reduced for non-negligent pre-1989 exposure
Application of Stokes v GKN and Thompson v British Shiprepairers
linked_authorities: Stokes v GKN (Bolts and Nuts) Ltd [1968] 1 WLR 1776
Allen v British Rail Engineering Ltd [2001] ICR 942

statutes_considered.title: Planning (Listed Buildings and Conservation Areas) Act 1990

enrichment.short_title: Coutts v Sebestyen: OFT determination and unauthorised overdraft credit
key_facts: Mr Sebestyen held a Coutts current account used for direct debits and accepted a £2,000 overdraft facility by letter in April 2002 at 8% interest.
From May 2002 the account remained persistently overdrawn beyond the agreed limit; Coutts continued paying debits and charged 26% unauthorised overdraft interest.
Coutts sued for about £20,074; Sebestyen argued Part V formalities and the OFT section 74 determination conditions were not satisfied.
Each payment beyond the credit limit was treated as a modifying agreement under section 82.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission limited to Consumer Credit Act and OFT Determination issues; OFT commented by letter.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; conditions (b) and (c) of the OFT Determination were satisfied by Coutts' April 2002 offer letter and June 2002 notification letters.
enrichment.ratio: OFT Determination conditions (b) and (c) are mutually exclusive: (b) applies to express overdraft agreements and (c) to tacit extensions; 'charges' means charges for granting credit not ordinary account or dishonour fees; condition (c) sets a deadline not a narrow notification window.
legal_issues: Whether section 82(4) disapplied OFT condition (c) for temporary excesses
Whether conditions (b) and (c) were mutually exclusive
Construction of 'charges' in the OFT Determination
Whether June 2002 letters prematurely failed condition (c)

enrichment.short_title: W v Acton Youth Court: civil ASBO procedure after driving convictions
key_facts: A 14-year-old pleaded guilty to vehicle offences and was made subject to a section 1C ASBO with wide prohibitions across England and Wales.
The prosecution relied on a same-day police statement detailing 32 incidents, much of it hearsay from reluctant residents.
The youth's solicitor had 12 minutes to take instructions after the statement was served; he did not seek a further adjournment.
Terms included bans on associating with persons committing offences and exclusion from named Northolt areas.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of Acton Youth Court's post-conviction section 1C ASBO, with Crown Court appeal adjourned pending this decision.
enrichment.outcome: Relief refused; proceedings held civil so hearsay admissible, but procedural criticisms left to Crown Court appeal; no finding of excess of jurisdiction.
enrichment.ratio: Section 1C ASBO proceedings are civil for Article 6 and hearsay purposes following McCann; while fairness requires adequate time to meet wide allegations, represented defendants who do not seek adjournment cannot complain the justices failed to adjourn of their own motion.
legal_issues: Whether section 1C ASBO proceedings are civil or criminal
Admissibility of hearsay under the Civil Evidence Act 1995
Whether insufficient adjournment vitiated jurisdiction
Whether ASBO terms were too wide or insufficiently clear
linked_authorities: R (McCann) v Crown Court at Manchester [2003] 1 AC 787
Gough v Chief Constable of the Derbyshire Constabulary [2002] QB 459
B v Chief Constable of Avon and Somerset Constabulary [2001] 1 WLR 340

enrichment.short_title: Hackney v Campbell: costs after failed possession and right-to-buy claim
key_facts: Hackney sought possession of Flat D, 43 Upper Clapton Road, contending Mrs Campbell had lost her tenancy and right to buy.
Mrs Campbell succeeded on the right to buy; her son Lawrence Campbell's separate counterclaims on repairs, harassment, human rights and adverse possession failed.
The judge awarded both Campbells their costs, treating Lawrence as having had a case throughout because of Hackney's conduct.
Lawrence Campbell's adverse possession claim targeted freeholders who were not parties; Hackney held only a leasehold interest.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against county court costs order following two-and-a-half day possession trial.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; Lawrence Campbell's costs order set aside and replaced with no order as to costs on his defence and counterclaim.
enrichment.ratio: Where a tenant succeeds on possession/right-to-buy but a co-defendant fails on separable counterclaim issues, costs should reflect issue-based success; without a workable percentage apportionment and where possession failed, no order may better reflect justice than awarding all costs to the unsuccessful counterclaimant.
legal_issues: Whether the judge erred in treating Lawrence Campbell as equally successful
Whether Hackney's conduct justified his costs award
Whether adverse possession against non-parties could succeed
Appropriate CPR costs order where counterclaim issues were peripheral at trial
linked_authorities: English v Emery Reimbold & Strick Ltd [2002] 1 WLR 2409

enrichment.short_title: R v Barnham: hidden assets and Drug Trafficking Act confiscation
key_facts: Barnham was convicted of two conspiracies to evade cannabis importation and sentenced to 11 and 9 years; benefit was assessed at £1,525,615.
Undercover officers recorded discussions of large-scale Moroccan cannabis importation and money laundering from 1995 to 1998.
At the realisable assets stage Barnham and his wife gave evidence the judge found untruthful; no credible account was given of hidden proceeds.
The judge ordered confiscation equal to assessed benefit because Barnham failed to prove lower realisable assets.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against confiscation order with leave of the Full Court after two-stage benefit and assets hearings.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed only to reduce the order by £65,000 for double-counting refurbishment expenditure already included in the house value; otherwise order upheld.
enrichment.ratio: At the second stage of confiscation the persuasive burden shifts to the defendant to prove realisable assets; the prosecution need not establish a prima facie case of hidden assets, but the judge must stand back to avoid serious injustice under Benjafield.
legal_issues: Whether Article 6 required the prosecution to prove hidden assets at stage two
Whether failed conspiracies meant drug stocks could not be realisable assets
Whether allowance should be made for co-conspirators' contributions
Whether £65,000 refurbishment was double-counted in benefit and house value
linked_authorities: R v Barwick [2001] 1 Cr App R (S) 445
Phillips v United Kingdom (2001) Application No 41087/98

enrichment.short_title: R (D) v SSHD: Article 2 public inquiry after near-fatal prison suicide
key_facts: D, a known suicide-risk remand prisoner at HMP Pentonville, hanged himself on 27 December 2001 and suffered irreversible brain damage.
An internal Draper investigation report was critical but key records and annexes were lost or destroyed.
The Secretary of State proposed a private inquiry by Mr Shaw without powers to compel witnesses or allow full participation by D's representatives.
Potential civil negligence proceedings and the prior internal inquiry were argued to satisfy Article 2 investigative obligations.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review claim by the Official Solicitor as litigation friend seeking a public Article 2 compliant inquiry.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded in principle: proposed private inquiry inadequate; tailored declarations granted on participation and disclosure; permission to appeal given to the Secretary of State.
enrichment.ratio: A near-miss suicide of a prisoner known to be at real and immediate risk engages the same Article 2 investigative standards as a death in custody; a private inquiry lacking public scrutiny, compellability, and meaningful family participation cannot satisfy Jordan, Edwards and Amin, and prior internal or civil proceedings did not displace that obligation here.
legal_issues: Whether Article 2 required a public inquiry after a non-fatal custodial suicide attempt
Adequacy of the Draper investigation and proposed Shaw inquiry
Relevance of potential civil proceedings and lost prison records
Required level of legal funding and family participation
linked_authorities: R (Amin) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2003] UKHL 51
